\chapter{Pero --- Two True Things at Once}
\label{ch:pero}
\hlchaptermodality{218}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can hold two facts against each other without denying either.}

I can hold two facts against each other without denying either.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[pero]{pero — the word that lets two true things stand together}

\label{lesson:ES-C58-pero}



\begin{quote}
With \emph{porque} you can give a reason: one thing \textbf{because of} another. That word makes two facts agree.

Now you need the opposite tool — the one for two facts that \textbf{do not} agree, and are both true anyway.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — one flick of the tongue, not the rolled \emph{rr}. \textbf{pero} = \emph{PEH-ro}. (The rolled version is a different word entirely, so this flick is worth getting right.)
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{pero} was \textbf{two} Latin words: \textbf{per hoc} — \emph{by this}, \emph{through this}.

You can still feel the route it took. \emph{By this} became \emph{for all that}, and \emph{for all that} is already a contrast: I grant you the first thing, and here is the second anyway. The phrase wore down into one short word and kept only the contrast.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Estoy cansado, \textbf{pero} estudio.}
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Notice what \emph{pero} does \textbf{not} do. It does not deny the first half. \emph{Estoy cansado} stays true — tiredness is not cancelled by studying.

That is the whole job: two things that pull in opposite directions, both standing. \emph{Porque} fuses two facts into one reason; \emph{pero} keeps two facts apart and admits both. Between them you can say almost anything.

And it is the first word of every argument you will ever make. Nobody argues by listing things they agree with.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Estoy cansado, pero estudio}
  \item something true about today, then \emph{pero}, then something that pulls the other way
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Porque} joins two facts into one reason. What does \emph{pero} do with two facts? (\textbf{Keeps them apart, and admits both.})

And what were its two Latin words? (\emph{\textbf{Per hoc}} — \emph{by this}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
